entries.text: * «LAM-ALIF» ( «لا» ) is a special shape showing lam ( «ل» ) joined to alif or hamzah ( «ا ء» ). It is not a separate letter. * As its name suggests, «LAM-ALIF» is read as lam first, then alif. The right side represents lam and the left side alif.

entries.text: «Tanween:» When the same vowel mark is placed twice on a letter, it is called tanween. When continuing the recitation, the letter ends as though followed by a noon with sukoon ( «نْ» ). There are three kinds of tanween: double fathah, double kasrah and double dammah.

entries.text: * An alif is usually written to the left of a letter with double fathah. * This alif is not pronounced when continuing, but acts as a lengthening letter when stopping. entries.text: ALIF - LAM

entries.text: We saw that lam-alif (لا) is used when a word requires lam (ل) followed by alif (ا).
entries.ttsText: We saw that lam-alif (Lam Alif) is used when a word requires lam (Lam) followed by alif (Alif).

entries.text: If alif (ا) followed by lam with sukoon (لْ) occurs at the beginning of a word, it is called the alif-lam article, or simply the “al” article (اَلْ).
entries.ttsText: If alif (Alif) followed by lam with sukoon (Lam) occurs at the beginning of a word, it is called the alif-lam article, or simply the “al” article (Alif Lam).

entries.text: Here, the alif (ا) before lam (ل) functions as a hamzah because it can carry a vowel. Remember that a vowelled alif with no lengthening function is called hamzah.
entries.ttsText: Here, the alif (Alif) before lam (Lam) functions as a hamzah because it can carry a vowel. Remember that a vowelled alif with no lengthening function is called hamzah.

entries.text: The following letter determines how lam is pronounced. If it is one of the letters (ء ب ج ح خ ع غ ف ق ك م و هـ ى) in the phrase (أَبْغِ حَجَّكَ وَخَفْ عَقِيمَهُ), lam is pronounced with sukoon. These letters are half of the 28 letters of the Quran.
entries.ttsText: The following letter determines how lam is pronounced. If it is one of the letters (Hamzah Ba Jeem Ha Kha Ayn Ghayn Fa Qaf Kaf Meem Waw Ha ) in the phrase (Abghi hajjaka wa khaf aqeemahu), lam is pronounced with sukoon. These letters are half of the 28 letters of the Quran.

entries.text: Some hamzahs at the beginning of a word lose their vowel when read together with the preceding word or letter, as though no hamzah were present. They are written as an alif without a vowel mark (ا). Sometimes a small connecting mark (ٱ) shows that they are not pronounced. These are called hamzat al-wasl. Examples:

entries.text: Sometimes the letter ta (ت) is written as “ta marbutah”: (ة ، ـة). This occurs only at the end of a word. It is written (ـة) when joined to the previous letter and (ة) when unjoined.
entries.ttsText: Sometimes the letter ta (Ta) is written as “ta marbutah”: (Ta marbutah Ta marbutah). This occurs only at the end of a word. It is written (Ta marbutah) when joined to the previous letter and (Ta marbutah) when unjoined.

entries.text: When stopping on a word ending in ta marbutah, it is pronounced like ha with sukoon (ـهْ). When continuing to the next word, it is pronounced as ta with its vowel.

entries.text: How Do We Stop on a Vowelled Letter at the End of a Word?
entries.ttsText: How Do We Stop on a Vowelled Letter at the End of a Word?

entries.text: When reading the Quran, we usually stop at the ends of verses, at stopping marks, or when we need to breathe. These stops can only be at the ends of words.
entries.ttsText: When reading the Quran, we usually stop at the ends of verses, at stopping marks, or when we need to breathe. These stops can only be at the ends of words.

entries.text: We do not stop by pronouncing fathah, kasrah or dammah. If the final letter is not already vowel-free—with sukoon or as a lengthening letter—its vowel is omitted and it is pronounced as though it had sukoon.
entries.ttsText: We do not stop by pronouncing fathah, kasrah or dammah. If the final letter is not already vowel-free—with sukoon or as a lengthening letter—its vowel is omitted and it is pronounced as though it had sukoon.

entries.text: For tanween, the rule is as follows: With double fathah written alongside alif, one fathah is removed. The letter is read with a single fathah, lengthened for two counts.
entries.ttsText: For tanween, the rule is as follows: With double fathah written alongside alif, one fathah is removed. The letter is read with a single fathah, lengthened for two counts.

entries.text: • When stopping on a hamzah with double fathah written without alif, it is also lengthened for two counts, as though an alif were beside it.
entries.ttsText: When stopping on a hamzah with double fathah written without alif, it is also lengthened for two counts, as though an alif were beside it.

entries.text: • On letters with double kasrah or double dammah, we stop with sukoon.
